‘My classroom was 30C. No one was learning. Then I started to feel dizzy’ – This is climate breakdown
As a UK heatwave intensified in early summer this year, the health impacts began to worsen. This is Gill’s story
Location: London, UK
Disaster: UK heatwave, 2026
Gill (not her real name), 43, is a teacher in London. In 2026, during the hottest summer on record, she suffered a seizure after experiencing heat exhaustion while teaching. The heatwave was made worse by the climate crisis.
The heat has always made me feel anxious and uncomfortable, but this year was different. The temperature was building up as the summer went on and as it was escalating it was becoming more and more frightening.
It was impossible to get any meaningful rest because I couldn’t fall asleep and when I did, I would wake up feeling suffocated because the air was so thick and dry and hot and there was nothing I could do to make myself feel better. Drinking water, using a fan, it didn’t help.
It got to the point where I would wake up feeling like I couldn’t breathe and with this rising sense of panic where I couldn’t really imagine how I was going to get through the day. I felt unsafe.
There was a lot of anxiety among my colleagues too. People were obviously very uncomfortable, they were worried about the kids, worried about themselves.
One day in late June I woke up and I was exhausted and was lacking the motivation that I normally have for work.
I got to work and my classroom was 30C. It used to be the photocopier room but because of demand for space they took the photocopier out. It’s a very small room with no windows. It was never designed to be a classroom, it’s got no ventilation.
No one was really learning and I was dealing with challenging behaviour and as the day went on I started to feel increasingly unwell to the point where I was dizzy and feverish and I had a really bad headache. I felt like I couldn’t concentrate on anything.
I was diagnosed with epilepsy about 20 years ago. It took about a year to get on top of it, but since then it’s not something that affects my life in any way, it’s extremely well controlled. But on this day, I had my first absent seizure since the diagnosis.
The best way to describe it is like pressing pause on the TV remote. I was on my lunch break and there was a pause and then it was like I restarted again a few seconds later.
I went to meet my colleague in reception, and she told me I had a lot of symptoms of heat exhaustion. I was feverish, I felt cold but my skin was really hot to touch, I was unable to regulate my body temperature and was fluctuating between being really hot and really cold.
No matter how much water I was drinking, I was just feeling chronically thirsty. I’ve never experienced anything like this before, it was really scary.
I was supposed to be teaching that afternoon, but I was not able to, so I cancelled the lesson and stayed in first aid.
My partner picked me up from work and that evening, like every evening over the summer, I just wasn’t really able to do anything. I spoke with my GP a few days later and they said as there is no obvious alternative explanation, they think I had the seizures because of the heat.
The next day, after the government issued its first red heat health alert of the year, the school announced it was closing at 12pm. I still came in though, I think there’s just a sense with teaching that we’re all in it together.
I’ve always found the heat uncomfortable but when you hear advice that those with medical conditions are vulnerable, I never really thought it applied to me. This year felt unprecedented. The relentlessness of it just sent me into a spiral.
It got to the point where I was reluctant to make plans in July and August. I don’t commit to things because I’m worried about the heat.
I already feel like my own life and experience is somewhat limited and then I look at a child in front of me and I think, what is their life going to be like when they’re my age?
Summers could soon be unrecognisable, how bad is it going to get? That question really haunts me. Particularly when I think about the young children in my family, my niece, my nephew, the young kids I teach. It’s frightening to think about how serious it’s got in the last five years, and then think, well, you know, five or 10 years from now, what will it be like then?
I have to try quite hard not to think about that too much because if I let those thoughts reach a natural conclusion I just feel really panicked, it’s terrifying.

10 kg of Kesar mangoes to cost ₹3,000 this year:25% drop in crop expected as warmer weather affects flowering
Farmers are worried as mango trees have not blossomed sufficiently and on time.
Night-time temperatures usually begin to drop between Navratri and Diwali, marking the ideal period for mango trees to flower. However, despite Diwali having arrived this year, temperatures at night have not fallen as expected.
This unusual weather pattern is affecting mango cultivation in the Sasan Gir region. The flowering normally seen on mango trees during this period has yet to appear.
Due to the adverse weather conditions, the mango crop is expected to be around 25% lower this year. The decline in production could directly affect market prices, meaning consumers may have to pay more for Gir's famous Kesar mangoes.
Condition of the mango orchards in the Sasan Gir area.
Scanty rainfall and changing weather affect mango flowering
Farmer Bipinbhai Jadav said mango trees usually begin flowering during this period, with early blossoms appearing every year. However, irregular weather and a shortage of rainfall have delayed flowering this season. Blossoms have appeared on only a few trees and in very small quantities.
The lack of the required cold conditions is also affecting the flowering process. Farmers are worried that even if the trees blossom now, cloudy skies and the possibility of unseasonal rain could further damage the crop.
Bipinbhai added that scanty rainfall has significantly reduced water levels in wells and borewells, making it difficult for farmers to provide adequate water to mango trees. Due to the shortage, the fruits that develop may not grow fully or attain the expected size.
Considering these factors, the Sasan Gir region is expected to record a 20% to 25% decline in mango production this year. With the crop likely to be significantly lower, prices of Gir Kesar mangoes could rise sharply in the coming season. A 10-kg box is expected to cost between Rs 2,500 and Rs 3,000.
Farmers are also struggling with persistent heat during both the day and night, along with fluctuating weather conditions.
Bhaskar reporter Vanraj Chauhan
Temperature fluctuations and changing rainfall patterns disrupt mango trees' natural cycle: Expert
Dr D.K. Varu, Principal and Dean of Junagadh College of Horticulture, said mango farmers have been facing such conditions for the past four to five years, with climate change being a major factor behind the problem.
Significant temperature fluctuations and changes in rainfall patterns have disrupted the natural physiological cycle of mango trees.
Under normal conditions, most mango trees flower in November, particularly after November 15. A night-time temperature of around 15°C and daytime temperatures between 20°C and 25°C are considered ideal for flowering. Dry weather after flowering, along with adequate sunlight, is also essential for a good harvest.
High temperatures could directly affect this season's mango crop
According to Dr Varu, temperatures have remained unusually high, with the mercury touching 40°C in October this year. Even in November, temperatures have continued to hover between 30°C and 35°C.
Although low rainfall this year has been somewhat favourable for mango cultivation, the excessively high temperatures are proving harmful. He said the trees are healthy, while the limited growth of new flushes, or copper-coloured leaves, has allowed the branches to mature. This is considered a positive sign for flowering.
Dr Varu said that if temperatures fall slightly and there is no severe cold spell after November 15 and during December, the trees could produce excellent flowering.
Gir Kesar mango prices likely to rise amid expected fall in production
Experts said that reports of mango orchards being cut down need to be viewed in context. Only very old and non-productive mango trees are being removed.
At the same time, new mango orchards are being developed rapidly in emerging growing areas of Saurashtra, including Bhesan, the Barda region of Ranavav, Savarkundla and Jesar.
However, unfavourable weather, low rainfall, inadequate water availability and high temperatures are expected to limit Gir Kesar mango production this year. With supplies likely to remain low, market prices could rise significantly above normal levels, leaving consumers with higher bills for the popular variety.

full_text:
University of Johannesburg researchers believe artificial intelligence (AI) could help African farmers protect livestock from extreme heat and drought by studying the bacteria in animals’ digestive systems.
The researchers say combining AI with information about the gut microbes of indigenous African animals could help farmers identify early signs of stress, improve animal health and increase the production of meat and milk.
The proposal comes as climate change, rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns place increasing pressure on livestock farming, particularly for small-scale farmers who cannot afford expensive animal feed and veterinary medicines.
In a study published in the journal Agriculture on August 12, researchers Dr Keabetswe Tebogo Ncube and Dr Fidele Tugizimana outline a roadmap for using AI and information about animals’ gut microbes to improve livestock nutrition and help animals cope with difficult farming conditions.
The study, titled “From Microbiomes to Precision Livestock Nutrition: An AI-Enabled Policy Roadmap for Africa”, argues that Africa needs to develop its own AI systems using information collected from local livestock and farming environments.
The researchers say indigenous African cattle, goats, sheep and chickens are naturally better equipped to survive extreme heat and drought than many breeds developed outside the continent. However, though these animals are more resilient and often require fewer medications, they tend to gain weight more slowly than breeds specifically developed for higher meat and milk production.
The technology can scan the animal, know that this animal is stressed, and trigger fans to blow mist so that the animal can cool down
— Dr Keabetswe Tebogo Ncube
Ncube, a researcher at UJ’s Research Centre for Plant Metabolomics, said many animals in rural areas were already experiencing stress because of the conditions in which they were raised. Cows, sheep and goats belonging to subsistence farmers often walk for hours in the heat to reach communal grazing areas. By the time they arrive, they are sometimes too exhausted to eat properly.
“Such an animal is going to focus more on survival than producing meat or milk, because the priority is to survive,” she said.
The researchers said that extreme heat and drought also affect the quality of grazing. Plants may produce fewer vitamins, minerals and proteins, which animals need to produce milk and meat.
This is where the bacteria living in animals’ digestive systems become important. According to Tugizimana, director of UJ’s Research Centre for Plant Metabolomics, these microbes respond to changes in the chemicals found in the plants animals eat.
“Those gut microbes will communicate among themselves that the balance of the chemicals in the plants has changed. The microbes then send their own chemical signals (metabolites) to the animal they live in, that there is a problem,” he said.
These chemical signals can affect how animals produce proteins, vitamins and other nutrients, potentially reducing milk production and affecting their health. The researchers believe studying these changes could help identify early warning signs of stress and allow farmers to intervene before animals become seriously affected.
They argue that AI systems trained using information about African livestock could help predict which animals are more likely to struggle during periods of extreme heat. Ncube said AI systems already used in some commercial farming operations could identify stressed animals and automatically activate cooling systems.
“The technology can scan the animal, know that this animal is stressed, and trigger fans to blow mist so that the animal can cool down,” she said.
However, she warned that technology developed for animals in other parts of the world might not work in African farming environments.
“In Africa, most of the livestock on small farms are indigenous cows, sheep and goats. These animals do not stay in one place. They have to walk long distances to eat. Also, the animals, the climatic systems and the farming systems are different. What we need to do is collect lots of data and then train our own AI data models.”
The researchers said the ultimate goal is to develop affordable tools that can support both commercial and smallholder farmers
Tugizimana used Nguni cattle as an example of how locally developed AI systems could help farmers make better decisions. He said the breed was naturally strong under heat stress, but information about its genetics and gut microbes could help researchers identify animals that might need additional support during extreme temperatures.
“We can tell this specific cow doesn’t have this marker. It may get too stressed under the heat. Rather, let’s start preparing it or do something different to support it before it gets too stressed,” he said.
The researchers believe small-scale farmers could also benefit from the proposed technology, even if they cannot afford expensive automated farming systems. For example, farmers could be advised to move their animals to grazing areas earlier in the morning and return later in the day to avoid the hottest hours.
Better information about indigenous livestock could also help researchers develop affordable feed supplements suited to local farming conditions.
The study notes that developing reliable AI systems will require more research and information collected from different African farming environments. This would include:
blood samples to study stress responses and genetic characteristics;
milk samples to monitor changes in milk quality; and
rectal swabs to examine the bacteria and chemical signals in animals’ digestive systems.
Researchers would also need information about weather conditions, feeding patterns, animal weights, births and deaths.
The researchers acknowledge that Africa still faces challenges, including:
limited research infrastructure;
shortages of specialised skills; and
a lack of reliable livestock data.
They propose a phased approach, beginning with building local datasets and research capacity before testing and validating AI systems across different breeds and farming environments. The researchers said the ultimate goal is to develop affordable tools that can support both commercial and smallholder farmers.
They argue that combining AI, livestock genetics and gut microbiome research could help improve animal health, reduce dependence on antibiotics and strengthen food production as climate conditions become increasingly unpredictable.

Weipa recorded its hottest November day on record on Saturday. Photo: Ugurhan Betin.
An emergency health warning remains in place as much of Cape York Peninsula and the Gulf swelters through a severe heatwave.
It comes after the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) revealed Weipa recorded its hottest November day on record on Saturday at 39.8 degrees celsius.
The national forecaster has warned weather conditions pose a health risk to the communities of Weipa, Mapoon, Aurukun, Pormpuraaw and Kowanyama, Maramie and northern Carpentaria Shire. Northern and western parts of Mareeba Shire have also been impacted.
It’s expected the heatwave will last until at least Thursday (12 November), but hotter than normal conditions could stretch to Monday or beyond.
On Wednesday morning, the BOM reported it was 32 degrees in Weipa, but forecast the mercury could reach as high as 39 degrees later in the day.
BOM meteorologist David Crock said “warmer air persists further north” and there would be “temperatures two to six degrees above average for central and northern Queensland”.
He said temperatures were “reaching up into the mid-30s for all the major centres along the east coast: Rockhampton, Mackay, Townsville and Cairns”.
“Showers and storms (are) confined really to only the far west of Queensland, where temperatures are really heating up into the 40s,” he said.
“Many of these northern districts are seeing severe heatwave conditions, which are persisting right through the week.”
The Cape is no stranger to sweaty conditions, but this record-breaking heatwave has sparked health warnings. Photo: Cape York Weekly/Luke Mortimer.
Queensland Health has urged affected residents to keep an eye on themselves and their loved ones. Heat stress can cause cramps, heat exhaustion and heatstroke.
Anyone concerned about their health, or their friends and family, should phone 13 HEALTH (13 43 25), or visit a local GP. In an emergency, immediately phone triple zero.
Queensland Health will issue an updated heatwave health warning if advice changes.
Heatwave tips
Monitor the weather using the Bureau of Meteorology’s Heatwave Service
Try to stay indoors during the hottest part of the day. Avoid strenuous activities
Don’t leave children or pets in parked cars
Keep in contact with elderly friends, neighbours and relatives during a heatwave
Close windows and doors to keep the heat out, and use air conditioning if possible
If you have to go outside, be sun safe by wearing a hat, long sleeves and light clothing. Take water, seek shade where possible and apply sunscreen every two hours
Drink water regularly and stay hydrated (between six and eight glasses each day)
Store food and medication at a safe temperature
Follow your doctor’s advice if you have any medical conditions
Avoid alcoholic, hot or sugary drinks including tea and coffee (they can make dehydration worse).

Only the district of Faro remains under a red warning for gusts, which could reach 120 km/h and, in the most exposed areas, up to 140 km/h.
In the districts of Lisbon, Setúbal and Beja, gusts of 100 km/h are forecast, potentially reaching 120 km/h in the most exposed areas, such as higher mountain ranges and coastal areas.
The remaining districts in Alentejo and central Portugal are under yellow gust warnings, with winds estimated at 90 km/h.
“The warning for Lisbon was brought forward and downgraded,” Patrícia Gomes added, saying that warnings in the districts of Lisbon, Setúbal and Faro will remain in place until 6 pm.
Regarding rainfall in these districts, red precipitation warnings remain in place, with only Évora downgraded to orange. “These warnings end at 6 pm in the southernmost parts of the country, while in the north they end at 9 pm,” the meteorologist added, stressing that further adjustments may be made throughout the day.
Forecasts of worsening weather conditions prompted the Government to decide to close schools and advise people to limit travel and work remotely wherever possible.

RED alerts have been activated across Spain as Storm Charles batters the country, forcing the closure of schools and parks along the southern coast.
The subtropical system has triggered maximum level warnings on the Canary Island of La Palma, as well as in parts of Caceres and Avila, bringing torrential rain and hurricane-force winds.
In Andalucia, the state weather agency AEMET has placed the Costa del Sol and Malaga city under an orange alert until midnight tonight (Wednesday).
Up to 80mm of rain is expected to fall in 12 hours across the Sol and Guadalhorce areas, prompting Malaga city hall to close all fenced parks and activate a local emergency plan.
Inland, Ronda is also under an orange warning with up to 100mm of rain forecast across the day.
Further west, authorities have suspended classes in 30 coastal municipalities across Cadiz, Huelva and the Strait of Gibraltar.
The closures affect heavily expat-populated towns including Algeciras, La Linea de la Concepcion, San Roque and Tarifa, as wind gusts threaten to reach 120km/h.
AEMET has also warned of a 40% to 70% chance of tornadoes or waterspouts forming off the coasts of Cadiz and Huelva before midnight.
Ports in both provinces will remain closed until 10pm, with waves of up to six metres forecast in the Atlantic and five metres in the Strait.
The regional government’s emergency coordination centre has already logged 195 incidents across Andalucia since Monday night, with Sevilla and Cadiz the worst affected.
Meanwhile, residents in La Palma described the conditions as ‘brutal’ as the storm lashed the island’s capital, Santa Cruz.
Charles is the second major storm to hit the country in just three days, following closely behind Storm Bruna.
